result.note: Tests the methodology changes in MoSPI's revised national accounts series (double deflation, price basket, base year) and the IMF's grading of India's data.

questions.prompt: Consider the following statements about the revised national accounts series that the Ministry of Statistics (MoSPI) launched in February 2026:
items: It adopts double deflation, which separately adjusts input and output prices to capture real value added.
The price basket used for deflation expands from 180 items to 600.
The deflators are drawn only from the wholesale price index (WPI) series.
questions.ask: How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explain: The third statement is wrong because the expanded basket draws on both the CPI and WPI series. Critics had argued that the earlier WPI-only approach inflated growth when global commodity prices fell but domestic consumer prices held.
questions.source: The price basket expands from 180 items to 600, drawing from both the consumer price index (CPI) and wholesale price index (WPI) series.

questions.prompt: In February 2026, MoSPI launched a revised national accounts series. What is the new base year of this series?
questions.explain: The base year moves to 2022-23 from 2011-12. The revision also replaces single deflation with double deflation.
questions.source: The base year moves from 2011-12 to 2022-23.

questions.prompt: In late 2025, which international institution graded India's national accounts statistics a "C"?
questions.explain: The IMF gave India's national accounts a "C" grade in late 2025. TBB notes this is a liability for a country marketing itself as a top investment destination, and the revised series aims to better reflect economic reality.
questions.source: The IMF graded India's national accounts a "C" in late 2025.
